s1.p1: Every new browser tab opens a live cryptocurrency chart. Track what you hold, read your country's crypto tax rules, practise with no real money, and get told when a price you care about is hit — with no permission asked at install.
s2.p4: Line or candlesticks over six ranges, with a price scale and a time axis. Drag it any way — sideways through time, up and down through prices — scroll or pinch to zoom where you point, and finer candles load as you go in. A log axis, an average that says what it covers, the US inflation, jobs, Fed and PCE releases marked where they fall, and every point readable from the keyboard.
s2.p6: Lines, trend lines, rays, boxes and notes that stay with the coin at their price and time. A ruler that says the change, the time and how often a move that far happened in that long. A line can become a price target.
s2.p8: Volume by price, where the price sits in each range, the usual range ahead as a cone, regimes and the levels where it has turned. Each was tested on years of history first, and each says what it counts — never what comes next.
s2.p10: Another coin, the S&P 500, the Nasdaq 100 or gold, from a drawer beside the chart. Both drawn as percent change from the same moment on one shared axis, with the gap, how often they stepped the same way and how closely they moved — so where the lines cross is where the market put them.
s2.p12: Sixteen chart patterns — head and shoulders, triangles, wedges, ranges, flags — twelve strategy setups and twenty-one readings such as divergences, the Ichimoku cloud and Fibonacci retracements, named where they appear. Each sits beside what followed it on this coin and how it did when tested on four coins. Counted, never scored.
s2.p14: The right of the chart becomes a board of squares — real price bands at real moments ahead, each with its chance, worked out from the coin's own history and checked against years of past squares before it was allowed on. Drag the board to look further, click a square twice, and it settles itself: called it, or missed. Any settled call replays over the price it settled on, and your record says how often chance alone would have done as well. The score is local, worth nothing, and never leaves.
s2.p16: "BTC rises above 80,000", or "BTC falls 5% in 1h, 4h or 24h". Reported next time you open a tab — even a move that happened and reverted overnight — and, only if you switch it on, as a Chrome notification.
s2.p18: Holdings by amount, or a public address read for its balance. Dated purchases, sales and income; cost basis by FIFO, LIFO or HIFO; the return month by month. Press <kbd>H</kbd> and the amounts are masked.
s2.p20: The crypto tax rules of 244 countries and territories — what is taxed and what is not, the rates, the tax year — each read from the country's own tax authority or law, linked and dated. Where none was confirmed, it says so. Not tax advice.
s2.p22: A perpetual-contract terminal priced from a real venue's public quotes and order book: long or short up to 200x, limit and stop orders, stops and take-profits dragged on the chart, funding and liquidation, a guide that names what is missing, and every contract you close kept. In simulated USDT that cannot be bought or cashed out — no real money, ever.
s2.p24: Fourteen sources, filtered to your coins or your holdings, with advertising kept out and one story written up four times shown once. Point at a sharp move on the chart and it marks the stretch that moved, with what was written about it ranked first. Click a headline and the story opens beside the list without its pictures, with a reading of it: what kind of story its words make it, the coins and figures it names, and what the chart did since. Counted, never judged.
s2.p26: What followed every past time this coin entered the state it is in now — with the count behind every figure, and no comparison at all below twelve episodes. It opens on what came after everything true right now, and lists the twenty past stretches most like the last month with what followed each, and every month of every year as a grid — tested, and no month stood apart, so none is called better. What got built instead of buy and sell signals.
s2.p28: Fear & Greed, market overview, halving, difficulty, fees, gas, RSI, funding, open interest, liquidations, long/short, alt season, regimes, options, US spot bitcoin ETF flows, stablecoins, watchlist, top movers and more. Add them from a gallery at small, medium or large — a bigger card shows more — hold one for its size, and pin up to four to the home screen, where they rest as outlines.
s2.p30: 81 coins, 37 currencies, 13 languages, dark / light / auto, blue and orange for colour-blind eyes, four modes, and a keyboard shortcut for everything — its letter on every tab, or hidden if you prefer. Press <kbd>?</kbd> to see them, or <kbd>/</kbd> to type a command — a coin and a range, a comparison, a target.
s2.h331: The next hour, by a model
s2.p32: A widget that gives Bitcoin's next hourly close as a band and a median, and a price target's chance of closing above it — from a volatility model fitted on years of hourly closes and tested on the twenty-one months it never saw, where 77.8% of hours closed inside its 80% band. It says that, and keeps its own score on your device.

s4.p66: PriceTab asks for no browser permission at install. No account, no analytics, no telemetry. Your coins, settings, portfolio, targets and practice account live in your browser's local storage and never leave the device — which is also why they don't follow you to another computer, unless you carry a backup file there yourself.
s4.p67: Prices come from public, keyless market APIs. The one thing that leaves the browser beyond a request for market data is a wallet address, and only if you paste one in to watch its balance — then it goes to that chain's balance provider and nowhere else. Checking it against the sanctions list happens on your device, from a list that ships with the extension. Two things are optional and off until you press a button inside the app: a Chrome notification for a hit target, and eight newsroom feeds.
s4.p68: It also means a target can only be checked while a PriceTab tab is open. Nothing runs in the background when your browser is closed: there is no background worker to run it.
s5.p74: A browser extension can read every page you open, so being suspicious of one is the correct instinct — including of this page, which is marketing. Below is the part that isn't: the manifest Chrome enforces, every host the code can reach, and three checks that take a minute each.
s5.div75: manifest.json — every key, long values shortened at …
s5.li76: Nothing to grant at install The permissions list is empty, so Chrome has nothing to ask you about when you add it. The two optional entries are asked for only when you press their button inside the app. That isn't a policy we promise to keep — it is the manifest, and the browser enforces it.
s5.li77: No content scripts It cannot read, change or even see the pages you visit. The extension exists on its own new tab and nowhere else.
s5.li78: Nothing runs in the background There is no service worker to run. Close the tab and the extension is not executing — which is also why a price target can only be checked when you open a tab.
s5.li79: Every network request is in two files src/api.js and src/widgets-data.js. (A third, src/i18n.js, reads a language file from inside the extension itself.) The source contains no XMLHttpRequest, no sendBeacon, no eval, no document.cookie, and no analytics SDK of any kind.
s5.li80: Requests go out, nothing about you goes with them There is no account, no device id and no telemetry endpoint. A price request contains a coin symbol and a currency code.

s5.div111: Check the permissions Open chrome://extensions, find PriceTab, click Details. The permissions list is empty, and there is no "service worker" link because there is no background page.
s5.div112: Watch the traffic Open a new tab, press F12, choose Network and reload. Every row will be one of the hosts above. With the widgets off, a first tab asks Coinbase for the price and the history of all six ranges — seven requests, so switching ranges is instant — and ten pages of six-hour bars for the next 24 hours' range: seventeen in all, measured on 9 Oct 2026. The next tab asked for nothing, because everything it needs is cached.
s5.div113: Read the code It ships unminified and unbundled, so what you install is what is on GitHub. grep -rln "fetch(" src/ returns three files: the two above, and the language loader, which only reads from the extension's own folder.
s6.p115: Click "Add to Chrome" — no sign-up, nothing to configure.
s6.p116: Open a new tab. Your live chart is already there.
s6.p117: Click the price to switch coins, or open settings to make it yours.
s7.p122: PriceTab is for information only and is not financial or tax advice. The derivatives account is a simulation in units with no value. Cryptocurrency prices are volatile and risky. Always do your own research.

foot.memory: This page remembers your theme, your language and whether you have seen what is new — in your browser's storage, on this device. It sets no cookie and sends none of it anywhere.
s2.tomorrow.p: Under the price: where it may be a day from now, as the range it should land in four times in five and the one it should land in half the time — from the same model as the board's squares. Tested once on 3,945 days across four coins it had never seen: 80.1% landed in the first range, 49.4% in the second. It also tried to say up or down, did no better than a coin toss, and so says neither.
s2.monitor.p: Press <kbd>M</kbd>: every coin you follow on one sortable table — the price, the day, the week and the month, where it sits in the month's range, how far it is from its high and how far it moves on a typical day — and how closely each pair has moved together, with the count behind it. A row opens its chart.
s2.phone.h: On your phone, as an app
s2.phone.p: The same page runs on the web. Open it on a phone and add it to the home screen: it opens full screen with its own icon, a tab bar for the chart, calls, targets and the portfolio, sheets that swipe away, and the side columns swiped in from the edges — clear of the browser's own back gesture. Nothing to install, and what you keep stays on the phone.
